record.original_question: Constructive mathematics is described here as mathematics together with the assumption that existence equals computability. Study constructions and objects from constructive mathematics from the viewpoint of program-size complexity, complementing earlier work based on dynamic complexities.

evidence.quote: Constructive mathematics is essentially mathematics plus the assumption that ‘existence = computability’. Constructions and objects in constructive mathematics have been studied from the point of view of dynamic complexities and it would be interesting to study them also from the point of view of program-size complexity. (C. Calude)

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Adopt the viewpoint of constructive mathematics, understood as ordinary mathematics together with the principle that "existence equals computability": every object asserted to exist must be presented together with an algorithm that produces it, and every proof of an existential statement must yield such an algorithm. For a finite binary string x, let K(x) denote its program-size (Kolmogorov) complexity, i.e. the length of a shortest program that outputs x on a fixed universal prefix-free Turing machine; extend K to finitely presentable mathematical objects via standard encodings. Existing work has analyzed constructive objects and constructions through "dynamic" complexity measures (such as time and space complexity of the algorithms witnessing existence).

Develop a systematic theory of constructive mathematics from the point of view of program-size complexity. Concretely:

(a) For canonical classes of constructive objects (e.g. constructive real numbers, constructive metric spaces, recursive functions, constructively presented algebraic structures, and witnesses produced by constructive existence proofs), define and study natural program-size complexity invariants attached to them.

(b) Prove nontrivial upper and lower bounds on the program-size complexity of objects arising from standard constructive theorems (e.g. constructive versions of the intermediate value theorem, the fundamental theorem of algebra, fixed-point theorems, or completion constructions).

(c) Identify constructive principles or theorems whose constructive content can be measured or separated by program-size complexity in a way that is not captured by dynamic (time/space) complexity, thereby producing a complement to the existing dynamic-complexity analysis of constructive mathematics.
